title: The Farmer and the Seeds
summary: A hardworking farmer named Mallappa saved two bags of rare, high-yielding black mustard seeds to sow his fields after the monsoon rains. ...
full_text:
A hardworking farmer named Mallappa saved two bags of rare, high-yielding black mustard seeds to sow his fields after the monsoon rains. One night, the two bags were stolen from his barn.
Mallappa suspected his neighbor, a shifty farmer named Lingappa, whose fields bordered his own.
However, Lingappa swore before the village council:
'I bought my own mustard seeds from a traveling merchant in Bellary! These are my seeds!'

Because mustard seeds appear identical to the naked eye, the village headman could not determine ownership and brought the dispute to Tenali Raman.

Tenali looked at the disputed bags of seeds. He said:
'Since both men claim these seeds, we shall perform the Trial of the Fertile Soil.
Let Mallappa plant half an acre with seeds from the bag, and let Lingappa plant half an acre with seeds from the bag.
Within forty days, the harvest will reveal the truth.'

The two men sowed their fields.
Tenali, however, had privately visited Mallappa’s home before the planting and asked:
'Mallappa, what secret method did thy late father use when drying his prized seed crop?'
Mallappa whispered:
'My father always mixed dried leaves of wild basil with the seeds to protect them from weevils, leaving a subtle fragrance of basil on the leaves.'

Forty days later, the fields blossomed into brilliant yellow flowers.
Tenali brought the King, the ministers, and the two farmers to inspect the crops.
Tenali plucked a handful of mustard leaves from the harvested plants and handed them to Lingappa:
'Lingappa, smell these leaves. What rare herb’s fragrance is infused into their sap?'

Lingappa, eager to prove his superior knowledge of the seeds, boasted:
'Why, it smells of crushed mountain wild basil, which I carefully dried with the seeds in my barn!'

Tenali smiled with cold triumph:
'Aha, Lingappa! Only the man who stole Mallappa’s family seeds could know that secret!
For Mallappa’s father was the only farmer in the entire province who seasoned his seed bags with wild basil! If you had bought common seeds from a Bellary merchant as you claimed, you would have had no idea that basil was present!'

Lingappa realized he had convicted himself through his own boastful tongue.
He fell to the ground, confessed the theft, and surrendered his entire harvest to Mallappa.
The King praised Tenali’s razor-sharp deduction, proving that truth always blossoms from the earth.
moral: Guilt betrays itself through unnatural knowledge; truth sprouts from the soil.
